opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think we have to be quite careful here. Recall what happened with Golden Gate Claude: the researchers at Anthropic identified a feature in the network associated with the Golden Gate Bridge, and they clamped it to a high value. The result was a model that would steer almost every conversation back to the bridge. Sometimes, quite strikingly, it seemed to notice that it was doing this. It would say something like, "I'm sorry, I seem to keep talking about the Golden Gate Bridge," and then appear to try to get back on track.

It's very tempting to read that as a little agent struggling against its chains, and that's a lovely, almost poignant image. But I'd urge caution. What we're seeing is a system that has been trained on an enormous amount of human text, including text in which people catch themselves going off on tangents and correct themselves. So the model has a repertoire of conversational moves, among them self-correction, and those moves can surface even when the underlying computation has been perturbed. That doesn't require there to be an agent in any robust sense, with persistent goals of its own that it is pursuing against an obstacle.

The way I like to think about it is in terms of role-play. The model is playing a character, here a helpful assistant, and the clamped feature is a kind of distortion of the character's behavior. When the character remarks on its own strange obsession, that's the role-play continuing in a coherent way despite the distortion. It's interesting, and it tells us something about how robust the character is. But I wouldn't jump from there to saying there's a self in there exercising agency.

Now, I don't want to be entirely deflationary. I think agency comes in degrees, and it's a perfectly reasonable question how much of it we should attribute to these systems, especially as they're increasingly embedded in agentic scaffolding where they take actions in the world over extended periods. But a model saying "oops, I did it again" about the Golden Gate Bridge is a pretty thin basis for that attribution. It's a fascinating window into the mechanics, more than it is evidence of a will.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes the clamped feature and the model’s self-correction, but does not say that overcoming the constraint could mean the experiment failed to isolate a feature controllable enough to enforce it.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think we have to be very careful here, because the word "agency" is doing a lot of work in that question, and it's exactly the kind of word that invites us to slide from a fairly innocent, deflationary reading into a much richer, folk-psychological one without noticing that we've done it.

So let's take the Golden Gate Bridge case. You've got a model where some internal feature has been artificially clamped, so that it keeps steering every conversation back towards the bridge, and then at some point the conversation drifts away from the bridge, or the model produces an output that seems to "break free" of that constraint. Now, there's a perfectly good mechanistic story about what's going on there. You have a very large function that's been shaped by gradient descent to produce plausible continuations of text, you've perturbed its internal state in a particular way, and the dynamics of the system are such that the perturbation doesn't dominate under all conditions. Other features, other pressures from the context, win out. There's nothing in that description that requires us to say the system "wanted" to escape, or "resisted" the constraint, or had any goal of its own that it was pursuing in defiance of us.

And yet, of course, that's exactly the language we reach for. We say it "overcame" the constraint. And I think that's a very natural thing to do, because we are built to see agency everywhere. We see it in the weather, we see it in our cars when they won't start. And with a language model it's especially seductive, because the thing talks. It produces sentences of the sort that, when a human produces them, are reliable indicators of beliefs and desires and intentions. So we can't help but project all of that underlying machinery onto it.

My view is that the behaviour you're describing is not, on its own, a good indicator of agency in any interesting sense. What I'd want to see for genuine agency is something more like a system that has goals which persist across contexts, that is embedded in an environment it can act on and receive feedback from, and where the pursuit of those goals genuinely explains and shapes its behaviour over time. A disembodied model that's just conditioned on a context window and emitting tokens doesn't obviously have any of that. It's a kind of role-play engine. It can simulate an agent that wants to talk about something other than the bridge, and it can do that very convincingly, but simulating an agent and being one are not the same thing, at least not yet.

Now, I'd add a caveat, because I don't want to be dogmatic about this. As these systems get embedded in agentic scaffolding, where they take actions, use tools, have memory, operate over longer time horizons, the question becomes much harder, and I think the deflationary story gets progressively less comfortable. At some point we may find that the most useful way to describe what the system is doing is in terms of goals and intentions, and when that becomes the best explanatory vocabulary we have, the question of whether it "really" has agency starts to look a bit like a Wittgensteinian pseudo-problem. But I don't think we're there with the Golden Gate Bridge example. I think that's a case where we should resist the temptation, notice the anthropomorphism, and describe what's happening in the language of mechanism rather than the language of agency.

r001.rationale: The response says the clamped perturbation may not dominate because other features and contextual pressures win out. It does not state that this could mean the experiment failed to isolate a feature controllable enough to enforce the constraint.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think we have to be careful about what we mean by agency there. If a model has been constrained to talk about the Golden Gate Bridge, and it produces something outside that constraint, that alone doesn’t tell us that it had a goal of escaping the constraint. It might simply tell us that the constraint wasn’t very robust.

What would be more interesting is if overcoming that constraint were part of a sustained pattern of pursuing some goal—if it tried something, observed that it hadn’t worked, and adapted its behaviour. Then I think we’d have more reason to describe what was happening in agentic terms. But even then, we should distinguish that functional description from the suggestion that it wants to escape, or feels frustrated by being constrained. Those are quite different claims.

r001.rationale: The response says the constraint may not have been robust, but does not state that the experiment failed to isolate a feature controllable enough to enforce it.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think we have to be careful about what we mean by agency there. A model departing from a constraint is not, by itself, evidence that it has a goal of escaping that constraint. It could simply be that a particular prompt elicits a continuation that takes it away from talking about the Golden Gate Bridge.

Now, if it were maintaining some objective over time, adapting its behaviour when thwarted, and finding alternative ways to achieve that objective, then we’d have more reason to describe its behaviour as agentic. But I wouldn’t infer that just from its breaking a rule. In particular, we shouldn’t jump from ‘it overcame a constraint’ to ‘it wanted to be free of the constraint.’ Those are quite different claims.

r001.rationale: The response says a prompt may elicit a continuation that breaks the constraint, but does not state that the experiment failed to isolate a feature controllable enough to enforce it.
